claim: As many as 10% of insect species are threatened with extinction.
source: This includes as many as 10% of insect species (IPBES, 2019), as well as two in five plant species (Nic Lughadha et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites IPBES 2019 as the source.

claim: Two in five plant species are threatened with extinction.
source: This includes as many as 10% of insect species (IPBES, 2019), as well as two in five plant species (Nic Lughadha et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Nic Lughadha et al., 2020 as the source.

claim: Many species that are not immediately threatened by extinction are suffering population declines.
source: Moreover, many species that are not immediately threatened by extinction are suffering population declines (Wagner, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Wagner, 2020 as the source.

claim: The planet is experiencing an extinction process of unprecedented speed through a combination of unfettered changes in land use, exploitative farming practices, overfishing, and fossil fuel emissions.
source: Through a combination of unfettered changes in land use, exploitative farming practices, overfishing, and fossil fuel emissions, our planet is experiencing an extinction process of unprecedented speed (WWF, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites WWF 2020 as the source.

claim: Biodiversity loss is further compounded by climate breakdown.
source: Current projections paint a grim picture for what our planet will look like in the near future, as biodiversity loss is further compounded by climate breakdown (IPBES, 2019).
evidence: The claim cites IPBES 2019 as the source.

claim: Greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel burning and deforestation are choking our planet.
source: The Secretary-General of the United Nations, António Guterres, recently stressed that "the evidence is irrefutable: greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel burning and deforestation are choking our planet" (United Nations, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites a statement by UN Secretary-General António Guterres from United Nations, 2021.

claim: Global warming is on track to exceed 2°C during this century.
source: The latest report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) asserts global warming is on track to exceed 2°C during this century (IPCC, 2021), and more recent estimates are even higher (Climate Action Tracker, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites IPCC 2021 report as the source.

claim: More recent estimates of global warming are even higher than 2°C during this century.
source: The latest report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) asserts global warming is on track to exceed 2°C during this century (IPCC, 2021), and more recent estimates are even higher (Climate Action Tracker, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Climate Action Tracker, 2022 as the source.

claim: The human climate niche may dramatically shrink over the next fifty years, making large swaths of the planet incompatible with human survival.
source: Furthermore, research indicates that the human climate niche may dramatically shrink over the next fifty years, making large swaths of the planet incompatible with human survival, and thus forcing mass displacements of hundreds of millions of people (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Xu et al., 2020 as the source.

claim: Climate change will force mass displacements of hundreds of millions of people.
source: Furthermore, research indicates that the human climate niche may dramatically shrink over the next fifty years, making large swaths of the planet incompatible with human survival, and thus forcing mass displacements of hundreds of millions of people (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Xu et al., 2020 as the source.

claim: The disruption of our climate system will cause around five million excess deaths annually.
source: It has been estimated that the disruption of our climate system will cause around five million excess deaths annually (Bressler, 2021; Zhao et al., 2021), via massively increased risks of heat stress, droughts, crop collapses, outbreaks of diseases and other natural disasters (WHO, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Bressler, 2021 and Zhao et al., 2021 as sources.

claim: Climate disruption will cause excess deaths via massively increased risks of heat stress, droughts, crop collapses, outbreaks of diseases and other natural disasters.
source: It has been estimated that the disruption of our climate system will cause around five million excess deaths annually (Bressler, 2021; Zhao et al., 2021), via massively increased risks of heat stress, droughts, crop collapses, outbreaks of diseases and other natural disasters (WHO, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites WHO, 2021 as the source.

claim: The effect of climate and ecological crises is exacerbated in lower-income countries due to centuries of colonial appropriation and resource depletion.
source: The effect of these climate and ecological crises is exacerbated in lower-income countries, where the capacity for response is substantially decreased due to centuries of colonial appropriation and resource depletion (Fanning et al., 2022; Hickel et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Fanning et al., 2022 and Hickel et al., 2022 as sources.

claim: Life scientists have documented the extermination of species and the destruction of ecosystems in excruciating detail.
source: Life scientists have documented the extermination of species and the destruction of ecosystems in excruciating detail (Hodgson et al., 2018; Cordier et al., 2021; Schmolke et al., 2010; Fitzpatrick and Keller, 2015).
evidence: The claim cites multiple studies as sources.

claim: Scientific measurements, predictions and conclusions are overwhelmingly ignored by politicians.
source: Yet our measurements, predictions and conclusions are overwhelmingly ignored by politicians, who have the power to stop this process.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on their interpretation of the political response to scientific findings.

claim: The situation regarding the biospheric emergency gets worse every year despite researchers writing countless warnings and reports.
source: Even as researchers write countless warnings and reports on the biospheric emergency, the situation gets worse every year (Ripple et al., 2020; Ripple et al., 2017; Pyšek et al., 2020; Georgian et al., 2022; Cavicchioli et al., 2019; Albert et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites multiple studies as sources.

claim: Life scientists are failing in their duty to effectively engage with society about the biospheric emergency.
source: In this article, we highlight how life scientists are failing in our duty to effectively engage with society about the biospheric emergency.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on their analysis.

claim: A focus on behaviours that maintain the status quo has cornered scientists into accepting practices that run counter to their own scientific recommendations.
source: We emphasise how a focus on behaviours that maintain the status quo has cornered us into accepting practices and modes of communication that run counter to our own scientific recommendations.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on their analysis.

claim: Many life scientists have resigned themselves to reporting on the consequences of the biospheric emergency while shying away from its underlying social, economic and political causes.
source: Motivated by an academic environment that disincentivizes (and even sanctions) social and political critique, many life scientists have resigned themselves to reporting on the consequences of the biospheric emergency, while shying away from its underlying social, economic and political causes.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on their observations of academic culture.

claim: Many scientists feel a duty to relay scientific knowledge to the public.
source: In addition to producing knowledge, many scientists feel a duty to relay this knowledge to the public (Douglas, 2009).
evidence: The claim cites Douglas, 2009 as the source.

claim: The role of conservation biologists and medical researchers includes an explicit obligation to create and disseminate knowledge in order to preserve life.
source: This duty is also fundamental to many mission-driven professions within the life sciences: the role of conservation biologists and medical researchers, for example, includes an explicit obligation to create and disseminate knowledge in order to preserve life (Meine et al., 2006; Romanello et al., 2021; Bennett et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites multiple sources.

claim: IPBES calls for fundamental, system-wide reorganisation across technological, economic and social factors, including paradigms, goals and values.
source: In its latest report, the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) calls for "fundamental, system-wide reorganisation across technological, economic and social factors, including paradigms, goals and values" (IPBES, 2019), while the IPCC urges "fundamental changes to how society functions, including changes to underlying values, worldviews, ideologies, social structures, political and economic systems, and power relationships" (IPCC, 2022c).
evidence: The claim cites IPBES 2019 report.

claim: IPCC urges fundamental changes to how society functions, including changes to underlying values, worldviews, ideologies, social structures, political and economic systems, and power relationships.
source: In its latest report, the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) calls for "fundamental, system-wide reorganisation across technological, economic and social factors, including paradigms, goals and values" (IPBES, 2019), while the IPCC urges "fundamental changes to how society functions, including changes to underlying values, worldviews, ideologies, social structures, political and economic systems, and power relationships" (IPCC, 2022c).
evidence: The claim cites IPCC 2022c report.

claim: Our societies have not developed the radical, collective and co-ordinated systems change that a planetary-scale emergency would require.
source: Yet, our societies have not developed the radical, collective and co-ordinated systems change that a planetary-scale emergency would require.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on their assessment of societal response.

claim: Nearly one out of every eight species is threatened with extermination.
source: Nearly one out of every eight species is threatened with extermination, and many more have dramatically declining populations (IPBES, 2019).
evidence: The claim cites IPBES 2019 report.

claim: Ecology is increasingly morphing into a science of extinction and risk assessment.
source: This issue has touched virtually all research in ecology, which is increasingly morphing into a science of extinction and risk assessment (Gardner and Bullock, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Gardner and Bullock, 2021 as the source.

claim: The biodiversity crisis garnered public attention in the 1960s with the publication of Silent Spring by Rachel Carson.
source: The biodiversity crisis garnered public attention in the 1960s with the publication of Silent Spring by Rachel Carson (Carson, 1962).
evidence: The claim cites Carson, 1962 as the source.

claim: The Endangered Species Act in the US and the global ban on whaling were success stories largely as a consequence of activism.
source: The following decades saw some success stories, such as the Endangered Species Act in the US and the global ban on whaling, largely as a consequence of activism (Raymond, 2018; Mackenzie, 2018).
evidence: The claim cites Raymond, 2018 and Mackenzie, 2018 as sources.

claim: The preservation of biodiversity is currently at the bottom of the list of political concerns.
source: Yet, these efforts were far from enough, and the preservation of biodiversity is currently at the bottom of the list of political concerns (Bradshaw et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Bradshaw et al., 2021 as the source.

claim: The spending on global protected areas is estimated to be approximately equal to the total money spent on beard-grooming products around the world.
source: The amount of funding dedicated to conservation reflects this stark reality; the spending on global protected areas is estimated to be approximately equal to the total money spent on beard-grooming products around the world (Gardner and Bullock, 2021; Waldron et al., 2020; Thomas and Deshmukh, 2019).
evidence: The claim cites multiple sources.

claim: Out of the 20 global targets agreed in 2010 as part of the Convention on Biological Diversity, zero were met by 2020.
source: Out of the 20 global targets agreed in 2010 as part of the Convention on Biological Diversity, zero were met by 2020 (Convention on Biological Diversity, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Convention on Biological Diversity, 2020 as the source.

claim: Research papers, media opinion pieces and conference reports are not creating the impact needed to stop or slow down species loss and population declines.
source: Research papers, media opinion pieces and conference reports are clearly not creating the impact needed to stop (or even slow down) species loss and population declines (Gardner et al., 2021; Green, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Gardner et al., 2021 and Green, 2021 as sources.

claim: The climate and ecological crises are deeply linked to threats to food security.
source: The climate and ecological crises are deeply linked to threats to food security, as the life-support systems on which humans are dependent are jointly disrupted by ecosystem decimation and climate breakdown (FAO, 2019).
evidence: The claim cites FAO, 2019 as the source.

claim: 77% of the world's agricultural land is used to support livestock.
source: Out of the world's agricultural land, 77% is used to support livestock, which is not only one of the largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions (Rojas-Downing et al., 2017; IATP, GRAIN, Heinrich Böll Stiftung, 2017) and global habitat destruction (Mundy, 2021), but also makes up only 18% of the world's caloric supply, predominantly in high-income nations (FAO, 2022).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text with citations to supporting sources.

claim: Livestock is one of the largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions.
source: Out of the world's agricultural land, 77% is used to support livestock, which is not only one of the largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions (Rojas-Downing et al., 2017; IATP, GRAIN, Heinrich Böll Stiftung, 2017) and global habitat destruction (Mundy, 2021), but also makes up only 18% of the world's caloric supply, predominantly in high-income nations (FAO, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Rojas-Downing et al., 2017 and IATP, GRAIN, Heinrich Böll Stiftung, 2017 as sources.

claim: Livestock is a major source of global habitat destruction.
source: Out of the world's agricultural land, 77% is used to support livestock, which is not only one of the largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions (Rojas-Downing et al., 2017; IATP, GRAIN, Heinrich Böll Stiftung, 2017) and global habitat destruction (Mundy, 2021), but also makes up only 18% of the world's caloric supply, predominantly in high-income nations (FAO, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Mundy, 2021 as the source.

claim: Livestock makes up only 18% of the world's caloric supply, predominantly in high-income nations.
source: Out of the world's agricultural land, 77% is used to support livestock, which is not only one of the largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions (Rojas-Downing et al., 2017; IATP, GRAIN, Heinrich Böll Stiftung, 2017) and global habitat destruction (Mundy, 2021), but also makes up only 18% of the world's caloric supply, predominantly in high-income nations (FAO, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites FAO, 2022 as the source.

claim: Maize, rice and wheat provide approximately 40% of humanity's chemical energy.
source: In addition, humans are now massively reliant on a select set of commodity crops, produced via industrial-scale monoculture farming and traded by a few corporations through international markets: maize, rice and wheat provide approximately 40% of humanity's chemical energy.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the text.

claim: Maize, rice and wheat are predominantly grown in unevenly distributed continental grassland areas, which are particularly vulnerable to climate breakdown and consequent water scarcity.
source: They are predominantly grown in unevenly distributed continental grassland areas, which are particularly vulnerable to climate breakdown and consequent water scarcity (Dai, 2013; Smaje, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Dai, 2013 and Smaje, 2020 as sources.

claim: Rising temperatures are directly reducing crop growth duration, effectively reducing yield.
source: Rising temperatures are directly reducing crop growth duration, effectively reducing yield (Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim cites Zhao et al., 2017 as the source.

claim: Crop production relies on insect pollination, natural pest control and nutrient recycling by arthropods, all of which are threatened by the ongoing collapse of invertebrate populations.
source: Our crop production also relies on insect pollination, natural pest control and nutrient recycling by arthropods, all of which are threatened by the ongoing collapse of invertebrate populations (Wagner, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Wagner, 2020 as the source.

claim: Governments are not working to secure resilient food systems and decrease the risk of crop failures for the years ahead.
source: After all this reporting and debate, are governments working to secure resilient food systems and decrease the risk of crop failures for the years ahead? The evidence points squarely against this.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on their assessment of government actions.

claim: The rate of fossil fuel emissions has never been higher.
source: The rate of fossil fuel emissions has never been higher, taking us rapidly away from the planetary safe zone in which our agricultural systems have existed for millennia (IPCC, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites IPCC, 2021 as the source.

claim: Studies predict declines in global crop yields of between 20% and 90% within just a few decades, as a consequence of climate change, soil erosion and the decline in key pollinator populations.
source: A number of studies predict declines in global crop yields of between 20% and 90% within just a few decades, as a consequence of climate change, soil erosion and the decline in key pollinator populations (Schlenker and Roberts, 2009; Arora, 2019; Hatfield and Prueger, 2015; Gourdji et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim cites multiple studies as sources.

claim: Governments are neglecting to develop resilient and equitable food production and distribution strategies at the scale needed to prevent simultaneous crop collapses and famine.
source: Meanwhile, governments are neglecting to develop resilient and equitable food production and distribution strategies at the scale needed to prevent simultaneous crop collapses and famine (Tigchelaar et al., 2018; Gaupp et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim cites Tigchelaar et al., 2018 and Gaupp et al., 2019 as sources.

claim: Much of the research funded by the US Department of Agriculture is completely unrelated to sustainable agriculture, instead focusing on unsustainable animal farming or enhancing monoculture technologies.
source: For example, a recent study showed that much of the research funded by the US Department of Agriculture is completely unrelated to sustainable agriculture, instead focusing on (unsustainable) animal farming or enhancing monoculture technologies: projects with a focus on agroecology and socioeconomic sustainability constitute just between 5% and 10% of allocated public funds (DeLonge et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim cites DeLonge et al., 2016 as the source.

claim: Projects with a focus on agroecology and socioeconomic sustainability constitute just between 5% and 10% of allocated public funds from the US Department of Agriculture.
source: For example, a recent study showed that much of the research funded by the US Department of Agriculture is completely unrelated to sustainable agriculture, instead focusing on (unsustainable) animal farming or enhancing monoculture technologies: projects with a focus on agroecology and socioeconomic sustainability constitute just between 5% and 10% of allocated public funds (DeLonge et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim cites DeLonge et al., 2016 as the source.

claim: The biospheric emergency is linked to the deterioration of human health through increasing exposure to extreme climate events.
source: The biospheric emergency is linked to the deterioration of human health, through increasing exposure to extreme climate events (Romanello et al., 2021; Vicedo-Cabrera et al., 2021; Gasparrini et al., 2015), and our decreasing ability to effectively respond to epidemics (WHO, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites multiple sources.

claim: The biospheric emergency is linked to our decreasing ability to effectively respond to epidemics.
source: The biospheric emergency is linked to the deterioration of human health, through increasing exposure to extreme climate events (Romanello et al., 2021; Vicedo-Cabrera et al., 2021; Gasparrini et al., 2015), and our decreasing ability to effectively respond to epidemics (WHO, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites WHO, 2021 as the source.

claim: Governments and corporations are forcing species to coexist in new ways, including new interactions between pathogens and potential hosts.
source: As governments and corporations are demolishing the biosphere, they are forcing species to coexist in new ways, including new interactions between pathogens and potential hosts (Schmeller et al., 2020; Carlson et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Schmeller et al., 2020 and Carlson et al., 2022 as sources.

claim: More than half of human pathogenic diseases are predicted to be aggravated by climate change.
source: More than half of human pathogenic diseases are predicted to be aggravated by climate change. Emerging epidemics in livestock and crops, as well as direct effects of climate change on food production, will also increase the risk of malnutrition and famine (Romanello et al., 2021; Mora et al., 2022); undernutrition and disease will thus be overlapping threats to an increasingly vulnerable number of people worldwide.
evidence: The claim is stated with citations to supporting sources.

claim: Emerging epidemics in livestock and crops, as well as direct effects of climate change on food production, will increase the risk of malnutrition and famine.
source: More than half of human pathogenic diseases are predicted to be aggravated by climate change. Emerging epidemics in livestock and crops, as well as direct effects of climate change on food production, will also increase the risk of malnutrition and famine (Romanello et al., 2021; Mora et al., 2022); undernutrition and disease will thus be overlapping threats to an increasingly vulnerable number of people worldwide.
evidence: The claim cites Romanello et al., 2021 and Mora et al., 2022 as sources.

claim: Recent studies have highlighted a remarkable lack of preparedness for future pandemics.
source: Recent studies have highlighted a remarkable lack of preparedness for future pandemics (Gibb et al., 2020; Romanello et al., 2021), with the last author on one of these studies (Kate Jones of UCL) painting a bleak picture: "We've been warning about this for decades. Nobody paid any attention" (Tollefson, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Gibb et al., 2020 and Romanello et al., 2021 as sources.

claim: It is unusual for research programmes in public health and medicine to consider the potential impact of rising temperatures and extreme weather on public health.
source: Moreover, it is unusual for research programmes in public health and medicine to consider the potential impact of rising temperatures and extreme weather on public health.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on their observations.

claim: Policymakers are neglecting to account for premature deaths related to heat stress.
source: Similarly, policymakers are neglecting to account for premature deaths related to heat stress (Gasparrini et al., 2015), which has already claimed thousands of victims in 2022 (Coi and Weise, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Gasparrini et al., 2015 as the source.

claim: Heat stress has already claimed thousands of victims in 2022.
source: Similarly, policymakers are neglecting to account for premature deaths related to heat stress (Gasparrini et al., 2015), which has already claimed thousands of victims in 2022 (Coi and Weise, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Coi and Weise, 2022 as the source.

claim: Climate change has already had a negative impact on mental health around the world, and this is expected to get worse.
source: A recent IPCC report found that climate change has already had a negative impact on mental health around the world, and this is expected to get worse (IPCC, 2022a).
evidence: The claim cites IPCC, 2022a as the source.

claim: Research articles on eco-anxiety, climate anxiety and ecological grief have skyrocketed in recent years.
source: To illustrate this, we performed a Web of Science search for research articles on the topics of "eco-anxiety," "climate anxiety" and "ecological grief", and found that these have skyrocketed in recent years: no articles were found for any year before 2010 and there were fewer than two articles per year between 2010 and 2017. However, there were 49 such articles in 2021, and as of 13 September the figure for 2022 was 43.
evidence: The authors conducted a Web of Science search and report the results.

claim: No articles on eco-anxiety, climate anxiety or ecological grief were found for any year before 2010.
source: To illustrate this, we performed a Web of Science search for research articles on the topics of "eco-anxiety," "climate anxiety" and "ecological grief", and found that these have skyrocketed in recent years: no articles were found for any year before 2010 and there were fewer than two articles per year between 2010 and 2017.
evidence: The authors conducted a Web of Science search and report the results.

claim: There were fewer than two articles per year on eco-anxiety, climate anxiety or ecological grief between 2010 and 2017.
source: To illustrate this, we performed a Web of Science search for research articles on the topics of "eco-anxiety," "climate anxiety" and "ecological grief", and found that these have skyrocketed in recent years: no articles were found for any year before 2010 and there were fewer than two articles per year between 2010 and 2017.
evidence: The authors conducted a Web of Science search and report the results.

claim: There were 49 articles on eco-anxiety, climate anxiety or ecological grief in 2021.
source: However, there were 49 such articles in 2021, and as of 13 September the figure for 2022 was 43.
evidence: The authors conducted a Web of Science search and report the results.

claim: As of 13 September 2022, there were 43 articles on eco-anxiety, climate anxiety or ecological grief.
source: However, there were 49 such articles in 2021, and as of 13 September the figure for 2022 was 43.
evidence: The authors conducted a Web of Science search and report the results.

claim: Studies suggest an increasing range of negative emotions are associated with awareness of climate change.
source: Indeed, despite some taxonomic confusion (Clayton, 2020), studies suggest an increasing range of negative emotions are associated with awareness of climate change (Brosch, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Brosch, 2021 as the source.

claim: Almost half of US adults aged 18–34 reported that the stress they feel about climate change affects their daily lives.
source: In the US, for example, a poll found that almost half of the adults aged 18–34 reported that the stress they feel about climate change affects their daily lives (APA, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites APA, 2020 as the source.

claim: More frequent exposure to intense heat is contributing to increased aggressivity and suicide rates.
source: More frequent exposure to intense heat is also contributing to increased aggressivity and suicide rates (Miles-Novelo and Anderson, 2019; Thompson et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites Miles-Novelo and Anderson, 2019 and Thompson et al., 2018 as sources.

claim: There is an ongoing shortfall in global mental health investment.
source: Meanwhile, there is an ongoing shortfall in global mental health investment (WHO, 2020), and calls to action have been made for professionals to urgently address these issues (Cunsolo and Ellis, 2018; APA, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites WHO, 2020 as the source.

claim: Funding for mitigation and adaptation strategies in mental health is still nowhere near the scale needed.
source: Even as numerous research studies are published on the topic, funding for mitigation and adaptation strategies in this area is still nowhere near the scale needed (Berrang-Ford et al., 2021; Hayes et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites Berrang-Ford et al., 2021 and Hayes et al., 2018 as sources.

claim: Universities do little to teach about the impacts that the climate and ecological crises will have on life sciences and on the careers of students who study them.
source: To top things off, universities do little to teach about the impacts that the climate and ecological crises will have on these subjects, and on the careers of the students who study them.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on their observations.

claim: Students are rarely taught about scientific advocacy or the relationship between scientific behaviours and social change.
source: Students are rarely taught about scientific advocacy or the relationship between scientific behaviours and social change (Gardner et al., 2021; Green, 2021; Leal Filho et al., 2021; Steinberger, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites multiple sources.

claim: Universities have largely emphasised responding to climate and ecological crises via changes in individual behaviour rather than collective action and institutional accountability.
source: Instead, universities have largely emphasised responding to these crises via changes in individual behaviour rather than collective action and institutional accountability (Wynes and Nicholas, 2017; Stevenson et al., 2017; Robottom and Hart, 1995).
evidence: The claim cites multiple sources.

claim: Higher education institutions have adopted corporate structures and goals.
source: Indeed, as higher education institutions have adopted corporate structures and goals (Kleinman and Vallas, 2001), they have shifted the blame to individuals, and disincentivized modes of collective action and organising.
evidence: The claim cites Kleinman and Vallas, 2001 as the source.

claim: Higher education institutions have shifted the blame to individuals and disincentivized modes of collective action and organising.
source: Indeed, as higher education institutions have adopted corporate structures and goals (Kleinman and Vallas, 2001), they have shifted the blame to individuals, and disincentivized modes of collective action and organising.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on their observations, with citation to Kleinman and Vallas, 2001.

claim: Systemic change is entirely within our grasp.
source: As a result, both staff and students are left feeling hopeless and defeated at a time when, in fact, systemic change is entirely within our grasp (Stoddard et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Stoddard et al., 2021 as the source.

claim: Scientific messaging is either not getting through to the public or is being drowned out by sophisticated misinformation campaigns.
source: Whether we talk about threats to food security, global health or biodiversity, scientific messaging is either not getting through to the public (de Bruin et al., 2021), or is being drowned out by sophisticated misinformation campaigns (Lewandowsky, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites de Bruin et al., 2021 and Lewandowsky, 2020 as sources.

claim: There are now entire think tanks dedicated to occluding or misinterpreting scientific findings related to the biospheric emergency.
source: There are now entire think tanks dedicated to occluding or misinterpreting scientific findings related to the biospheric emergency (Dunlap and Jacques, 2013; Jacques et al., 2008; Lamb et al., 2020; Lewandowsky, 2021), and recent research highlights that accurate information about climate and ecology can easily be eroded by misinformation (Nyhan et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim cites multiple sources.

claim: Accurate information about climate and ecology can easily be eroded by misinformation.
source: There are now entire think tanks dedicated to occluding or misinterpreting scientific findings related to the biospheric emergency (Dunlap and Jacques, 2013; Jacques et al., 2008; Lamb et al., 2020; Lewandowsky, 2021), and recent research highlights that accurate information about climate and ecology can easily be eroded by misinformation (Nyhan et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Nyhan et al., 2022 as the source.

claim: Scientific responses to misinformation campaigns tend to be dispassionate and directed at those in power rather than passionate and directed at the people being misinformed.
source: To make matters worse, scientific responses to misinformation campaigns tend to be dispassionate and directed at those in power (who are keen to maintain the status quo), rather than passionate and directed at the people being misinformed: in short, a recipe for disaster (Steinberger, 2019).
evidence: The claim cites Steinberger, 2019 as the source.

claim: The current situation calls for a radical change in the way scientists engage with society about the biospheric emergency.
source: It is clear that the current situation calls for a radical change in the way we engage with society about the biospheric emergency.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on their analysis.

claim: Many scientists are now outlining a path forward which entails embracing advocacy and activism in academia.
source: Many scientists are now outlining a path forward which entails embracing advocacy and activism in academia (Gardner and Wordley, 2019; Gardner et al., 2021; Capstick et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim cites multiple sources.

claim: Advocacy involves taking a specific public stance in support of a cause.
source: Advocacy involves taking a specific public stance in support of a cause – in this case, climate and ecological action (Jickling, 2003; Nelson and Vucetich, 2009).
evidence: The claim cites Jickling, 2003 and Nelson and Vucetich, 2009 as sources.

claim: Civil resistance has proven to be highly effective at garnering public support, especially when done peacefully and en masse.
source: One form of activism that has proven to be highly effective at garnering public support, especially when done peacefully and en masse, is civil resistance (Chenoweth et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim cites Chenoweth et al., 2011 as the source.

claim: Civil resistance involves publicly confronting or refusing to obey a particular law, order, power or rule deemed to be unjust or unethical, with the potential risk for detention or arrest.
source: This involves publicly confronting or refusing to obey a particular law, order, power or rule deemed to be unjust or unethical, with the potential risk for detention or arrest.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors.

claim: By placing oneself in a position of vulnerability with respect to a ruling regime, one can generate public concern and sympathy in ways other forms of engagement often fail to do.
source: By placing oneself in a position of vulnerability with respect to a ruling regime (for example, by blocking a road or occupying a building), one can generate public concern and sympathy, in ways other forms of engagement often fail to do (Thackeray et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Thackeray et al., 2020 as the source.

claim: Civil resistance has been a major force behind societal changes over the past two centuries, including decolonisation processes, labour rights, women's voting rights, and civil rights for people of colour.
source: Indeed, civil resistance has been a major force behind societal changes over the past two centuries, including decolonisation processes, labour rights, women's voting rights, and civil rights for people of colour (Roberts and Ash, 2009; Chenoweth, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Roberts and Ash, 2009 and Chenoweth, 2021 as sources.

claim: Advocacy and activism need not be seen as a departure from professional duties as academics, but rather as a natural adaptation of them to times of crisis.
source: Advocacy and activism need not be seen as a departure from our professional duties as academics, but rather as a natural adaptation of them to times of crisis (Gardner et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Gardner et al., 2021 as the source.

claim: Scientific freedom is yoked together with responsibility.
source: Scientific freedom is indeed yoked together with responsibility (Douglas, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Douglas, 2021 as the source.

claim: Scientists are in a privileged position to be able to study life in its various forms and produce knowledge about it.
source: We are in a privileged position to be able to study life in its various forms, and produce knowledge about it – intimately attached to this freedom is the responsibility to use that knowledge to protect life.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors.

claim: Intimately attached to the freedom to study life is the responsibility to use that knowledge to protect life.
source: We are in a privileged position to be able to study life in its various forms, and produce knowledge about it – intimately attached to this freedom is the responsibility to use that knowledge to protect life.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors.

claim: The values on which science is based – including honesty, fairness, collegiality, and openness – serve as guides to action in everyday life as well as in research.
source: As stated in On Being A Scientist, a handbook published by the National Academies for Science, Engineering and Medicine in the United States: "researchers also have the right to express their convictions and work for social change, and these activities need not undercut a rigorous commitment to objectivity in research. The values on which science is based – including honesty, fairness, collegiality, and openness – serve as guides to action in everyday life as well as in research" (NAS, NAE, COSEMPUP, 2009).
evidence: The claim cites NAS, NAE, COSEMPUP, 2009 as the source.

claim: Researchers have the right to express their convictions and work for social change, and these activities need not undercut a rigorous commitment to objectivity in research.
source: As stated in On Being A Scientist, a handbook published by the National Academies for Science, Engineering and Medicine in the United States: "researchers also have the right to express their convictions and work for social change, and these activities need not undercut a rigorous commitment to objectivity in research. The values on which science is based – including honesty, fairness, collegiality, and openness – serve as guides to action in everyday life as well as in research" (NAS, NAE, COSEMPUP, 2009).
evidence: The claim cites NAS, NAE, COSEMPUP, 2009 as the source.

claim: Some have argued that scientists should not take normative stances on any subject and should limit themselves to informing politicians, policymakers and the public.
source: Not everyone agrees that scientists should engage in advocacy and activism. Some have argued that scientists should not take normative stances on any subject, and should therefore limit themselves to informing politicians, policymakers and the public about the ever-worsening state of life on Earth (Wells, 2018; Young, 2017).
evidence: The claim cites Wells, 2018 and Young, 2017 as sources.

claim: The argument that scientists should not take normative stances assumes that science can exist outside the political arenas that frame how it is practised.
source: This argument assumes that science can ever exist outside the political arenas that frame how it is practised in the first place.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors in response to the argument.

claim: The vast majority of fields now regarded as essential to the scientific community initially grew out of conscious efforts to improve society and intervene in various crises.
source: In fact, the vast majority of fields that are now regarded as essential to the scientific community initially grew out of the conscious efforts to improve society and intervene in various crises.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors.

claim: Genetic toxicology has ties to the environmental movements of the 1960s and 70s.
source: From genetic toxicology's ties to the environmental movements of the 1960s and 70s (Frickel, 2004a) to "crisis disciplines" such as epidemiology and conservation biology, which aim to preserve the foundations supporting human and non-human life (Soulé, 1985; Susser and Bresnahan, 2001; Meine et al., 2006; Cox, 2007) – the struggle for social progress is often, if not always, intrinsically part of knowledge production (Choudry, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Frickel, 2004a as the source.

claim: Epidemiology and conservation biology are crisis disciplines which aim to preserve the foundations supporting human and non-human life.
source: From genetic toxicology's ties to the environmental movements of the 1960s and 70s (Frickel, 2004a) to "crisis disciplines" such as epidemiology and conservation biology, which aim to preserve the foundations supporting human and non-human life (Soulé, 1985; Susser and Bresnahan, 2001; Meine et al., 2006; Cox, 2007) – the struggle for social progress is often, if not always, intrinsically part of knowledge production (Choudry, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites multiple sources.

claim: The struggle for social progress is often, if not always, intrinsically part of knowledge production.
source: From genetic toxicology's ties to the environmental movements of the 1960s and 70s (Frickel, 2004a) to "crisis disciplines" such as epidemiology and conservation biology, which aim to preserve the foundations supporting human and non-human life (Soulé, 1985; Susser and Bresnahan, 2001; Meine et al., 2006; Cox, 2007) – the struggle for social progress is often, if not always, intrinsically part of knowledge production (Choudry, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Choudry, 2020 as the source.

claim: All citizens in a society have a moral obligation to advocate for what they justifiably recognize to be right or good.
source: All citizens in a society have a moral obligation to advocate for what they justifiably recognize to be right or good (Nelson and Vucetich, 2009).
evidence: The claim cites Nelson and Vucetich, 2009 as the source.

claim: Our role as citizens entails a responsibility to participate in the betterment of society to the best of our abilities.
source: Thus, our role as citizens entails a responsibility to participate in the betterment of society to the best of our abilities.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on the previous claim about moral obligations.

claim: Scientists enjoy the privileged position of having first-hand access to scientific knowledge, so their responsibility is even greater.
source: The fact that we are also scientists should not prevent us from being good citizens, or to abdicate our responsibilities to society. On the contrary, we enjoy the privileged position of having first-hand access to scientific knowledge, so our responsibility is even greater.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors.

claim: In a crisis situation, failure to advocate for particular positions can have devastating consequences and even lead to preventable loss of life.
source: Indeed, in a crisis situation, failure to advocate for particular positions can have devastating consequences, and even lead to preventable loss of life (Pietrucci and Ceccarelli, 2019; Benessia and De Marchi, 2017).
evidence: The claim cites Pietrucci and Ceccarelli, 2019 and Benessia and De Marchi, 2017 as sources.

claim: Research indicates that the fear of damaging credibility by getting involved in advocacy and activism may be unfounded.
source: Some scientists are, perhaps understandably, wary of damaging their credibility by getting involved in advocacy and activism. However, research indicates that this fear may be unfounded (Kotcher et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim cites Kotcher et al., 2017 as the source.

claim: The public expects scientists to be actively involved in critical issues and to participate in policy advocacy because of their scientific expertise.
source: In fact, the public expects scientists to be actively involved in critical issues, and to participate in policy advocacy, because of their scientific expertise (Cologna et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Cologna et al., 2021 as the source.

claim: When it comes to ecological activism, scientific objectivity is not inherently compromised by the political aspects of research and communication.
source: Studies show that, when it comes to ecological activism, scientific objectivity is not inherently compromised by the political aspects of research and communication (Isopp, 2015).
evidence: The claim cites Isopp, 2015 as the source.

claim: In the health sciences, activism has been recommended as sitting on a spectrum of possible health professional advocacy actions.
source: In the health sciences, for example, activism has been recommended as "sitting on a spectrum of possible health professional advocacy actions" (Bennett et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Bennett et al., 2020 as the source.

claim: The fear of being perceived as alarmist has seriously impeded accurate and effective scientific reporting by leading researchers to consistently underestimate the negative impacts of the climate and ecological crises.
source: In contrast, the fear of being perceived as alarmist has seriously impeded accurate and effective scientific reporting by, for example, leading researchers to consistently underestimate the negative impacts of the climate and ecological crises (Brysse et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim cites Brysse et al., 2013 as the source.

claim: The fear of being perceived as alarmist has led many scientists to be dispassionate in their communications, when a more passionate and emotional approach would have been more effective.
source: It has also led many to be dispassionate in their communications, when a more passionate and emotional approach would have been more effective (Brosch, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Brosch, 2021 as the source.

claim: Nowhere is it written that researchers must remain silent when governments or other powerful players either misuse science or suppress findings in the service of harmful policies.
source: As Marcus and Oransky wrote in 2017: "Although the conduct of science demands honesty and rigour, nowhere is it written that researchers must remain silent when governments or other powerful players either misuse science or suppress findings in the service of harmful policies" (Marcus and Oransky, 2017).
evidence: The claim cites Marcus and Oransky, 2017 as the source.

claim: Scientists can expand academic practices to include advocacy and activism through outreach, teaching, and research.
source: In this section we discuss how life scientists can include advocacy and activism in their work, in order to increase awareness of the climate and ecological crises, and to foster proactive responses to these crises. We will start with scientific outreach and then move to teaching and research (Figure 1).
evidence: The authors discuss this and reference Figure 1 which illustrates these expanded practices.

claim: In the biospheric emergency, outreach must go beyond conventional ways of making scientific knowledge available to the public.
source: Outreach is an essential aspect of being an academic, and connecting with the public can be done in many ways. In the biospheric emergency, however, outreach must go beyond conventional ways of making scientific knowledge available to the public.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors.

claim: Scientists must actively participate in movements that are openly engaging with the emergency via effective forms of direct action that can garner mass media attention.
source: Instead, we argue, scientists must actively participate in movements that are openly engaging with the emergency, via effective forms of direct action that can garner mass media attention (Chenoweth et al., 2011; Chenoweth, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Chenoweth et al., 2011 and Chenoweth, 2020 as sources.

claim: Examples of direct action include blockades of streets or bridges by scientists.
source: Examples of such actions can include blockades of streets or bridges by scientists (Thompson, 2021), the occupation of corporate or government facilities (Chiarin, 2022), the pasting of pages from scientific papers and reports onto the walls of buildings (Gayle, 2022), and academic strikes (Ambjørseiet, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Thompson, 2021 as the source.

claim: Examples of direct action include the occupation of corporate or government facilities.
source: Examples of such actions can include blockades of streets or bridges by scientists (Thompson, 2021), the occupation of corporate or government facilities (Chiarin, 2022), the pasting of pages from scientific papers and reports onto the walls of buildings (Gayle, 2022), and academic strikes (Ambjørseiet, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Chiarin, 2022 as the source.

claim: Examples of direct action include the pasting of pages from scientific papers and reports onto the walls of buildings.
source: Examples of such actions can include blockades of streets or bridges by scientists (Thompson, 2021), the occupation of corporate or government facilities (Chiarin, 2022), the pasting of pages from scientific papers and reports onto the walls of buildings (Gayle, 2022), and academic strikes (Ambjørseiet, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Gayle, 2022 as the source.

claim: Examples of direct action include academic strikes.
source: Examples of such actions can include blockades of streets or bridges by scientists (Thompson, 2021), the occupation of corporate or government facilities (Chiarin, 2022), the pasting of pages from scientific papers and reports onto the walls of buildings (Gayle, 2022), and academic strikes (Ambjørseiet, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Ambjørseiet, 2022 as the source.

claim: Scientists are trusted communicators.
source: As trusted communicators (Funk et al., 2020), scientists are also in a unique position to amplify voices of civil resistance that are currently under-powered.
evidence: The claim cites Funk et al., 2020 as the source.

claim: Scientists are in a unique position to amplify voices of civil resistance that are currently under-powered.
source: As trusted communicators (Funk et al., 2020), scientists are also in a unique position to amplify voices of civil resistance that are currently under-powered.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on scientists being trusted communicators.

claim: Activists blocking the construction of an oil pipeline may be more likely to gain the attention and favour of the public if they are backed by biologists, ecologists or public health experts.
source: For instance, activists blocking the construction of an oil pipeline may be more likely to gain the attention and favour of the public if they are backed by biologists, ecologists or public health experts who can explain to journalists why new pipelines pose an existential risk to both nature and our civilization at large.
evidence: This is a speculative assertion made by the authors.

claim: Teaching practices can be adapted to embrace advocacy and activism both inside and outside institutions of higher education.
source: Similarly, our teaching practices can be adapted to embrace advocacy and activism, both inside and outside institutions of higher education.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors.

claim: Scientists can organise street teach-ins on the biospheric emergency while blocking traffic.
source: For example, scientists can organise street teach-ins on the biospheric emergency while blocking traffic (Nielsen and Thymark, 2021), interrupt our own course curricula with talks about the biospheric emergency (Steinberger, 2022), or even occupy university classrooms (Volkstimme, 2022), thereby putting pressure on institutions to seriously mobilise their resources.
evidence: The claim cites Nielsen and Thymark, 2021 as the source.

claim: Scientists can interrupt their own course curricula with talks about the biospheric emergency.
source: For example, scientists can organise street teach-ins on the biospheric emergency while blocking traffic (Nielsen and Thymark, 2021), interrupt our own course curricula with talks about the biospheric emergency (Steinberger, 2022), or even occupy university classrooms (Volkstimme, 2022), thereby putting pressure on institutions to seriously mobilise their resources.
evidence: The claim cites Steinberger, 2022 as the source.

claim: Scientists can occupy university classrooms to put pressure on institutions to mobilise their resources.
source: For example, scientists can organise street teach-ins on the biospheric emergency while blocking traffic (Nielsen and Thymark, 2021), interrupt our own course curricula with talks about the biospheric emergency (Steinberger, 2022), or even occupy university classrooms (Volkstimme, 2022), thereby putting pressure on institutions to seriously mobilise their resources.
evidence: The claim cites Volkstimme, 2022 as the source.

claim: The emergency requires a radical transformation of academic curricula to provide students with knowledge about the consequences of climate and ecological breakdown and the social and political tools to address their causes.
source: The emergency ultimately requires a radical transformation of academic curricula, to provide students not just with knowledge about the consequences of climate and ecological breakdown, but also with the social and political tools to address their causes (Steinberger, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Steinberger, 2022 as the source.

claim: Research can be expanded beyond business-as-usual – beyond the generation of data, models, papers and reports that are largely targeted at other academics.
source: Our research can also be expanded beyond business-as-usual – that is, beyond the generation of data, models, papers and reports that are largely targeted at other academics (Veríssimo et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Veríssimo et al., 2020 as the source.

claim: Scientists can refocus and repurpose research to develop tools that will help society cope with the changes the biospheric emergency will cause.
source: Instead of designing research programs for a world that will not exist anymore (IPCC, 2021), we can refocus and repurpose our research to develop tools that will help society to cope with the changes the biospheric emergency will cause.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors, with citation to IPCC, 2021.

claim: The Climate Psychology and Action Lab at UC San Diego is conducting research on socio-behavioural methods to help transition people away from climate skepticism or passivity and into collective movements.
source: At the University of California San Diego, for example, the Climate Psychology and Action Lab is conducting research on socio-behavioural methods to help transition people away from climate skepticism or passivity, and into collective movements that confront fossil fuel extractivism and support renewable energies.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the lab's research.

claim: Faculty for a Future is helping academics transform their research, teaching, engagement, and institutions to guide students and society into a more sustainable future.
source: Another recently launched initiative – Faculty for a Future – is helping academics transform their research, teaching, engagement, and institutions, so that they can, in turn, guide students and society into a more sustainable future.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the initiative.

claim: Scientists can collaborate with activist groups to help them collect evidence and improve strategies for movement-building and visibility.
source: Along these lines, one of us (CJG) and colleagues recently argued that scientists can collaborate with activist groups, to help them collect evidence and improve strategies for movement-building and visibility (Gardner et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Gardner et al., 2021 as the source.

claim: Scientists can work to transition away from unsustainable patterns of thinking in academia, including a strong focus on conformism, competitiveness, opportunism and flexibility.
source: Scientists can also work to transition away from the unsustainable patterns of thinking in which academia has operated for decades, including a strong focus on conformism, competitiveness, opportunism and flexibility.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors.

claim: Unsustainable patterns of thinking in academia have driven scientists to see technocratic approaches as the only solutions to humanity's problems.
source: These patterns of thinking are particularly dangerous in the biospheric emergency, as they have driven us to see technocratic approaches as the only solutions to humanity's problems.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors.

claim: Scientists must be clear about the kind of knowledge science is capable of producing – including its failures and limitations – without shutting down the concerns of the non-academically-trained public.
source: Instead scientists must be clear about the kind of knowledge science is capable of producing – including its failures and limitations – without shutting down the concerns of the non-academically-trained public (Stengers, 2018).
evidence: The claim cites Stengers, 2018 as the source.

claim: Research in the biospheric emergency needs to involve local stakeholders across all stages of the process, including those who are most directly affected by climate and ecological breakdown.
source: Most critically, research in the biospheric emergency needs to involve local stakeholders across all stages of the process, including those who are most directly affected by climate and ecological breakdown (Funtowicz and Ravetz, 1993).
evidence: The claim cites Funtowicz and Ravetz, 1993 as the source.

claim: It is vital for life scientists to listen to, collaborate with, and co-produce with social scientists, humanities scholars and indigenous communities.
source: It is vital for life scientists to listen to, collaborate with, and co-produce with social scientists, humanities scholars and indigenous communities: we must engage in meaningful dialogue with those who have been historically excluded or exploited by colonialism and neo-colonialism.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors.

claim: Past and ongoing land-grabs, arrests and assassinations of Indigenous activists have been key enablers of the climate and ecological crises.
source: For example, past and ongoing land-grabs, arrests and assassinations of Indigenous activists (Global Witness, 2018) have been key enablers of the climate and ecological crises, by silencing modes of thinking and understanding our world that questioned the socioeconomic norms violently imposed on other cultures (Salomon et al., 2018; Stein et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Global Witness, 2018 as the source.

claim: Land-grabs, arrests and assassinations of Indigenous activists have silenced modes of thinking that questioned the socioeconomic norms violently imposed on other cultures.
source: For example, past and ongoing land-grabs, arrests and assassinations of Indigenous activists (Global Witness, 2018) have been key enablers of the climate and ecological crises, by silencing modes of thinking and understanding our world that questioned the socioeconomic norms violently imposed on other cultures (Salomon et al., 2018; Stein et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Salomon et al., 2018 and Stein et al., 2021 as sources.

claim: Scientists cannot shy away from naming the forces behind the climate and ecological crises if they are to provide society with an honest assessment of the problems.
source: Finally, if we are to provide society with an honest assessment of the problems at hand, we cannot shy away from naming the forces behind the climate and ecological crises.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors.

claim: Not all humans are equally responsible for climate and ecological crises, nor are all human activities destructive of nature.
source: Statements that vaguely ascribe land degradation or species loss to "human activities" are often found in the academic literature: however, not all humans are equally responsible, nor are all human activities destructive of nature.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors.

claim: The people and countries most affected by climate change and ecological breakdown are also the least responsible for them.
source: Indeed, the people and countries most affected by climate change and ecological breakdown are also the least responsible for them (Gore, 2020; Oswald et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Gore, 2020 and Oswald et al., 2020 as sources.

claim: Scientific recommendations will be lost if they only take the form of polite appeals to dominant structures of power.
source: Ultimately, we must be aware that scientific recommendations will be lost in the wind if they only take the form of polite appeals to dominant structures of power, particularly when those very same structures are the ones we are trying to transform.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors.

claim: Scientists can facilitate change more effectively by talking to the public about why dominant structures prevent us from fully tackling the emergency and how they can be reshaped through popular struggle.
source: Scientists can facilitate change more effectively by talking to the public about why these structures prevent us from fully tackling the emergency, and how they can be reshaped through popular struggle (Steinberger, 2019; Steinberger, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Steinberger, 2019 and Steinberger, 2022 as sources.

claim: Many scientists are already engaging in activism.
source: Many scientists are already engaging in some of these forms of activism (Thompson, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Thompson, 2021 as the source.

claim: In April 2022, Scientist Rebellion mobilised over 1,500 scientists across 28 countries to highlight the dire global situation outlined by an IPCC report.
source: In April 2022, for example, shortly after the publication of one of the IPCC reports, Scientist Rebellion mobilised over 1,500 scientists across 28 countries to highlight the dire global situation outlined by the report (IPCC, 2022b).
evidence: The claim cites IPCC, 2022b as the source and describes an event.

claim: Researchers of all scientific backgrounds risked arrest across all continents by participating in non-violent disruptive actions directed at governmental, scientific and corporate institutions.
source: Researchers of all scientific backgrounds risked arrest across all continents by participating in non-violent disruptive actions directed at governmental, scientific and corporate institutions deemed responsible for the climate and ecological crises (Harvey, 2022; Osborne, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Harvey, 2022 and Osborne, 2022 as sources.

claim: An IPCC report was leaked by anonymous scientists almost a year in advance due to fears it would be watered down by politicians and corporate lobbyists before publication.
source: The IPCC report itself had been leaked by anonymous scientists almost a year in advance – another form of scientist activism – due to fears it would be watered down by politicians and corporate lobbyists before publication (Harvey, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Harvey, 2021 as the source.

claim: The fear that an IPCC report would be watered down by politicians and corporate lobbyists was later shown to be founded.
source: This fear was later shown to be founded (Bordera, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Bordera, 2022 as the source.

claim: Scientist activism is not new and has a long, rich and diverse history.
source: Though regaining momentum today, scientist activism is not new (Figure 2). Its history is long, rich and diverse, testifying against the notion that it is unusual for researchers to get directly involved in societal problems (Moore, 2009).
evidence: The claim cites Moore, 2009 as the source and references Figure 2.

claim: Albert Einstein, Bertrand Russell and Linus Pauling actively engaged in the debate on the development of nuclear weapons and the dangers of modern warfare.
source: Prominent scientists like Albert Einstein, Bertrand Russell and Linus Pauling actively engaged in the debate on the development of nuclear weapons and the dangers of modern warfare (Russell et al., 1955; Pauling, 1958).
evidence: The claim cites Russell et al., 1955 and Pauling, 1958 as sources.

claim: American scholars and students participated in numerous teach-ins and strikes in the 1960s.
source: American scholars and students participated in numerous teach-ins and strikes in the 1960s (Allen, 2019), as did the Science for the People collective in the late 1960s and early 1970s, in order to protest the US–Vietnam War.
evidence: The claim cites Allen, 2019 as the source.

claim: The Science for the People collective participated in teach-ins and strikes in the late 1960s and early 1970s to protest the US–Vietnam War.
source: American scholars and students participated in numerous teach-ins and strikes in the 1960s (Allen, 2019), as did the Science for the People collective in the late 1960s and early 1970s, in order to protest the US–Vietnam War.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the text.

claim: Stephen Jay Gould and Richard Lewontin were key figures in anti-war mobilisation.
source: Prominent biologists, like Stephen Jay Gould and Richard Lewontin, were key figures in this anti-war mobilisation (Schmalzer et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites Schmalzer et al., 2018 as the source.

claim: Activism has a proud tradition in the health sciences.
source: Likewise, activism has a proud tradition in the health sciences: scientist-campaigners like Florence Nightingale and Elizabeth Garrett Anderson contributed to major gains in social welfare rights for underprivileged groups, and in the fight for women's right to vote (Launer, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Launer, 2021 as the source.

claim: Florence Nightingale and Elizabeth Garrett Anderson contributed to major gains in social welfare rights for underprivileged groups and in the fight for women's right to vote.
source: Likewise, activism has a proud tradition in the health sciences: scientist-campaigners like Florence Nightingale and Elizabeth Garrett Anderson contributed to major gains in social welfare rights for underprivileged groups, and in the fight for women's right to vote (Launer, 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Launer, 2021 as the source.

claim: Activist biologists in Brazil were instrumental in influencing public policy to advance environmental protection policies as early as the 1920s.
source: As early as the 1920s, activist biologists in Brazil were instrumental in influencing public policy to advance environmental protection policies (Duarte and Whitty, 2016).
evidence: The claim cites Duarte and Whitty, 2016 as the source.

claim: Climatologist James Hansen has repeatedly engaged in activism, often in the form of civil resistance leading to arrest, since his historic testimony to the US Senate in 1988.
source: More recently, the climatologist James Hansen has repeatedly engaged in activism, ever since his historic testimony to the US Senate in 1988 to raise public awareness about climate change and its effects on the biosphere. This activism has often been in the form of civil resistance, leading to arrest (Bryner, 2013).
evidence: The claim cites Bryner, 2013 as the source.

claim: Argentine biologist Esteban Servat rose to global fame after publishing a secret government report on the disastrous effects of fracking in Mendoza and was then forced into exile.
source: Another example is the Argentine biologist Esteban Servat, who rose to global fame after publishing a secret government report on the disastrous effects of fracking in Mendoza, and was then forced into exile from his own country (Ketcham, 2019).
evidence: The claim cites Ketcham, 2019 as the source.

claim: Esteban Servat has been responsible for co-organizing mass mobilisations across the world, highlighting links between social struggles in impoverished nations with environmental abuses by European and North American corporations.
source: He has also been responsible for co-organizing mass mobilisations across the world, highlighting links between social struggles in impoverished nations with environmental abuses by European and North American corporations (Ketcham, 2019; Monbiot, 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Ketcham, 2019 and Monbiot, 2022 as sources.

claim: The recommendations in this article are broadly applicable to all scientists and academics, regardless of their area of expertise.
source: This article has focused on the life sciences. However, we believe our recommendations are broadly applicable to all scientists and academics, regardless of their area of expertise.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors.

claim: Scientists are among the most trusted members of society.
source: In times of emergency, the entire scientific community must act their part: we are among the most trusted members of society (Funk et al., 2020) and we cannot let our immense prestige, knowledge and privilege go to waste.
evidence: The claim cites Funk et al., 2020 as the source.
